summary: Describes the Triple DES-CBC security transform for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload. It applies the DES cipher three times to strengthen encryption. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Scrambling the message three times with the same lock method to make it harder to crack.

subtitle: How IPsec's ESP encrypts packets by running the DES cipher three times in a row with three keys.

tldr.problem: The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) needs a concrete encryption algorithm to protect IP datagrams, and single DES was seen as needing something stronger.
tldr.mechanism: Triple DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode processes each 8-byte block three times (encrypt, decrypt, encrypt) with independent keys, using an Initialization Vector carried in every datagram. Padding, a Pad Length octet and a Payload Type octet complete the encrypted portion.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines the payload layout and the encryption and decryption steps, and warns that security depends on the algorithm, the key management and correct implementations. It is Experimental.

today: RFC 1851 is an Experimental memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is not an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Triple DES for ESP
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 1827) provides confidentiality for IP datagrams by encrypting the payload data. This memo specifies how ESP uses a variant of the Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode of the US Data Encryption Standard (DES). The variant, Triple DES (3DES), processes each block of the plaintext three times, each time with a different key.

The reader is expected to know the Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol (RFC 1825), which defines the overall security plan for IP.
sections.eli5: Regular DES locks the message once. Triple DES locks it three times with three different keys.

sections.title: Keys, IVs and Block Size
sections.content:
The shared secret 3DES key is effectively 168 bits long. It consists of three independent 56-bit quantities, each stored as a 64-bit (eight octet) value whose least significant bit in each octet is a parity bit.

This mode needs an Initialization Vector (IV) of eight octets. Each datagram carries its own IV, so a datagram can be decrypted even when others are dropped or reordered. How IV values are chosen is implementation dependent. A counter starting at a random value is called acceptable, but the notes warn that cryptanalysis may exploit it, and that a pseudo-random generator needs a period long enough to avoid repetition during the session key's lifetime.

3DES works on blocks of eight octets, which often requires padding. Input and output have the same length, which allows in-place work. If the data to decrypt is not a multiple of eight octets, an error is indicated as described in RFC 1825. Three DES-CBC implementations can be pipelined in series, and the RFC notes that at least one hardware implementation could process about 1 Gbps at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: The three keys together make one big secret. Each message also carries a small random starter note so that scrambling the same words twice looks different.

sections.title: The ESP Payload Format
sections.content:
The ESP payload holds these fields in order: a 32-bit Security Parameters Index (SPI), the Initialization Vector, the Payload Data, Padding, a Pad Length octet and a Payload Type octet.

  • SPI: identifies the Security Parameters for the datagram and MUST NOT be zero.
  • IV: variable size, constant for all 3DES datagrams of the same SPI and IP destination, and a multiple of 32 bits. Sizes of 32 and 64 bits MUST be supported. With a 32-bit IV, the 64-bit IV is the 32-bit value followed by its bit-wise complement. The session key SHOULD be changed at least as often as 2**32 datagrams, even with a full 64-bit IV.
  • Payload Data: begins with the protocol header named by Payload Type. For IP-in-IP encapsulation (Payload Type 4) that is another IP header.
  • Padding: filled with implementation dependent, preferably random, values to align Pad Length and Payload Type at an eight octet boundary. It MUST be ignored after decryption.
  • Pad Length: the size of the Padding field, typically 0 to 7 but up to 255, which can hide the real data length.
  • Payload Type: the IP Protocol/Payload value of the contents. In tunnel mode it is 4.

Pad Length and Payload Type are opaque: they are set before encryption and examined only after decryption.
sections.eli5: Every package has a label saying which agreement it follows, a starter note, the secret contents, some filler to make it fit, and a note saying how much filler there is and what is inside.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption Steps
sections.content:
3DES here is a variant of DES-CBC where the DES function is replaced by an encryption, then a decryption, then an encryption, with independent keys k1, k2 and k3. When all three keys are the same, 3DES is equivalent to DES-CBC, so 3DES hardware can run in DES mode unchanged.

To encrypt: append padding so the length modulo 8 equals 6 (a 41 octet plaintext gets 5 octets of padding), append the Pad Length octet, append the Payload Type octet, provide an IV of the size indicated by the SPI, and encrypt with Triple DES in EDE mode. Then build the IP datagram with the SPI, IV and encrypted payload. The IP length reflects the encrypted data plus the SPI, IV, padding, Pad Length and Payload Type octets.

To decrypt: remove the SPI and use it to look up the negotiated parameters and key. Remove the IV, whose size the negotiation determines. Decrypt (the RFC calls this DED mode). Remove and check the Payload Type, and if it is unrecognized, discard the payload with an appropriate ICMP message. Remove the Pad Length and that many pad octets, adjust the IP length, and pass the result to the protocol named by Payload Type.
sections.eli5: To send, add filler and two notes, then lock it three times. To receive, unlock it three times, read the notes, throw away the filler and hand the contents to whoever it is for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The quality of the security depends entirely on the strength of Triple DES, the correctness of its implementation, the security of key management, the strength of the key, and correct implementations in all participating nodes. Applications may wish to avoid weak keys for any of the three DES rounds, though the odds of picking one at random are low.

DES has been shown not to be a group, so combining several rounds is not equivalent to one DES with a different key. Triple DES with independent keys is not as hard to brute-force as a cipher with three times the key length, because a space/time tradeoff breaks triple block encryption in the time naively expected for double encryption. Double DES falls to a meet-in-the-middle attack, so 3DES with independent keys is needed for this level of security. An attack on two-key 3DES is sixteen times faster than any known for independent keys.

CBC also permits a cut and paste attack: a damaged block garbles itself and the next block only, so an attacker with legitimate access to the same key may insert or replay data from other users. Ordinary transport checksums can detect this but are not cryptographically strong, so user or connection oriented integrity checking is needed (RFC 1826). Cryptanalysis may not use brute force at all, and the RFC advises watching developments and switching transforms if 3DES proves weak.
sections.eli5: Three locks are good but not three times as good. Someone clever might also swap pieces of messages around, so you need a separate check that nothing was tampered with.
